THOMAS HAGOS / MUSA 2026DAY 08 · UTOPIA

Aksum, Built

An imagined city, lived in.

Aksum, in northern Ethiopia, was the capital of a kingdom linking Africa, Arabia and the Mediterranean world. Its stone monuments still carry the language of its architecture: doors, windows and projecting beam ends.

What if that architectural language grew into a living city?

The evidence beneath the city.

Terrain: modern Copernicus GLO-30 surface model. Approximate landmark positions: © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL. Projection: UTM zone 37N, north foreshortened to 0.36. Towers, homes, colonnaded courts, people, riders and circulation are speculative. Garments and horses are interpretive entourage, not verified historical reconstructions. Animated paths do not represent excavated roads or measured journeys. Shaded relief is computed from the saved elevation grid; colors do not reconstruct ancient vegetation or stone types. Two monument sketches use UNESCO dimensions; the fallen stele’s orientation and carved details are schematic. Returned obelisk: UNESCO, 2008; Great Stele: UNESCO. Ninety pedestrians and six riders; figure size is increased for legibility.

Tower module: a chosen 6 m podium plus 4.32 m per storey, informed by Yeha reconstruction research. Nineteen chosen storeys gives 88.08 m; this is not evidence of ancient Aksum building heights or structural capacity. Historical periods follow UNESCO and The Met. No shared historical moment is implied.
